sentences.text: The name Segnosaurus translates to "slow lizard," while the species name galbinensis honors the Galbin region where it was found.
The nearly complete right half of the lower jaw measures 379 mm in length, 55.5 mm in height, and 24.5 mm in depth.
This animal is unique among all known theropods for having triple cutting edges on its teeth.
It possessed a massive humerus measuring 560 mm in length with an almost-cylindrical shaft.
Estimates suggest the creature reached lengths of 6 to 7 meters and weighed approximately 1.3 tons.
A pathological bone growth walled over the 14th tooth socket in the right lower jaw, though the specific cause of the damage remains unknown.
A 2020 study by Campione and Evans estimated the body mass between 4.2 and 4.6 tons, with a possible range of 3.1 to 5.8 tons.
In 2007, Martin Kundrát and colleagues identified dinosaur eggs with embryos of the type Dendroolithidae from China's Nanchao Formation as belonging to therizinosaurs.
These therizinosaur eggs were arranged in a circular structure without a central opening, touching each other.
Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens were found in the Gobi Desert during the 1970s, leading to the formal description of the genus in 1979.
A joint Soviet-Mongolian expedition uncovered a partial skeleton at the Amtgay locality within the Bayan Shireh Formation in 1973.
Segnosaurus and its relatives were likely slow-moving, mainly herbivorous animals, contrasting with the carnivorous nature of most other theropods.
Therizinosaurs like Segnosaurus likely used their long forelimbs, necks, and beaks for browsing and had large guts to process plant material.
Segnosaurians shared an opisthopubic pelvis, a slender mandible, and toothless front jaws.
Research from 1979 and 1981 suggested that Segnosaurus was not adapted for rapid movement due to its short, massive metatarsus and large, splayed toes.
Researchers Barsbold and Perle hypothesized that Segnosaurus and its relatives might have been amphibious.
Researchers Barsbold and Perle noted in 1979 and 1980 that therizinosaurs likely evolved in a different direction from typical predatory theropods.
Segnosaurus possessed unique dentary teeth with additional carinae and folded carinae featuring denticulated front edges.
The teeth had large, bulbous serrations with approximately 5 to 6 per 3 mm along the edges.
Segnosaurus replaced its teeth in waves moving from the back to the front of the jaws, involving two to three new teeth at a time.
Multiple nesting sites indicate that some therizinosaurs nested colonially, similar to hadrosaurs, prosauropods, titanosaurs, and birds.
Research confirmed that the family Segnosauridae is a junior synonym of the family Therizinosauridae.
In 1979, Perle proposed the new family Segnosauridae for Segnosaurus fossils.
In 1994, Perle and colleagues accepted the synonymy of Segnosauridae with Therizinosauridae and classified therizinosaurs as maniraptoran theropods related to modern birds.
Segnosaurus lived in southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 102 to 86 million years ago.
The presence of Nothronychus in North America during the Turonian stage suggests a faunal interchange between North America and Asia via a late-Early Cretaceous land bridge.
While split tooth edges are usually considered abnormalities in other theropods, in Segnosaurus this feature was uniform and likely served a functional purpose rather than being a defect.
Gregory S. Paul argued in 1984 that segnosaurs were derived prosauropods rather than theropods.
In 1995, Lev A. Nessov debated the theropod classification of therizinosaurs, arguing instead that they were a distinct group within Saurischia.
